items.body: On a Friday in mid-July, a delivery truck entered the Mirelle Bay Pool Supply yard, carrying a pallet of 48 jugs of liquid chlorinating solution. While a forklift carried the pallet to the covered dock, it fell and the load split open. Accounts differ on whether the fall was caused by broken paving or an uneven stack, but the accident resulted in multiple jugs bursting and liquid spreading toward a yard drain. Warehouse staff placed sand bags around the drain before responders arrived. Tessin Fire Service logged the call and arrived shortly after, washing remaining liquid into a temporary holding bund while firefighters in breathing apparatus moved surviving jugs under a tarpaulin. A licensed waste contractor's tanker collected the contained liquid the following morning. The business park air monitor registered chlorine above its alarm threshold, peaking before dropping back below the threshold later that afternoon. Yard cameras and gate logs captured the timeline of the delivery, the fall, and the immediate evacuation of workers upwind.

An incident occurred at the Veltrane Dye Depot on the Orsel Canal wharf when a fire broke out in the cold-storage annex shortly after 04:00 on 22 October. The annex smoke detector panel recorded an alarm on zone 2 before any other zone reported, with the first alarm raised at 04:06. Security camera footage time-stamped 04:09 showed the annex roller door glowing orange at its lower edge. Cameras on the north wharf subsequently lost power at 04:31. The first emergency call was logged at 04:12 by a passing canal barge pilot who described flames visible through the annex upper vents, and the first pumper left the fire station at 04:14. Five appliances were at the scene at the peak of the response. Firefighters drew water from the Orsel Canal using a floating suction hose, and the wharf road was closed until mid-morning. One firefighter was treated for a minor wrist burn. 

Imre Dallow, the sole supervisor on site, led six warehouse staff out through the loading door, and a subsequent headcount accounted for everyone within minutes. Dallow had noted the refrigeration compressors running normally during a 03:30 walk-round. The annex contained about 40 pallets of powdered pigment and refrigerated dye concentrate. An insurance loss adjuster estimated that the annex roof collapsed entirely while the main warehouse suffered only smoke and water damage.

An operational review of the power failure at Kestrel Ridge Observatory shows that the grid supply to the site dropped out at 00:58, prompting the standby generator to start automatically about twenty seconds later. The generator ran for 38 minutes before shutting down at 01:36. During this period, the dome shutter had already been closed at 00:50 because of incoming snow, and the single access road to the ridge was closed by snow that night.

When the generator stopped, the battery-backed computers stayed on. Accounts of the subsequent power loss differ regarding the exact sequence of internal failures, and conflicting statements exist concerning whether the generator stopped due to low oil pressure or because its overheating protection tripped after snow blocked the cooling air intake. The controller recorded a stop event followed by a lockout state that required a manual reset. 

Site engineer Talwen Pryce walked through the snow from the staff cottage and reset the lockout at the generator panel, successfully restarting the unit at 02:04. Fuel tank records show no sudden drop in level between 01:00 and 02:10, confirming steady levels decreasing normally from sixty-one to forty-eight percent during the hour.

The main fibre link between Skerrin Isle and the mainland suffered a total loss of optical signal in a single reading at 11:52 p.m. on a Tuesday in late October, with no prior gradual decline or returning signal during the night. The island's normal main-link capacity of 1,000 megabits per second dropped to a microwave radio backup link rated at 20 megabits per second. The backup link began carrying island traffic at 11:53 p.m., one minute after the failure. Harbour Master Tobias Reld confirmed calm overnight sea conditions with winds below 10 knots and no vessels anchored near the cable route after dark. 

The on-duty engineer opened a priority two incident ticket at 12:20 a.m. and activated the backup radio link. A repair ship was requested from the mainland depot, though no arrival date is confirmed. The limited capacity caused widespread operational impacts. The Skerrin Isle School IT technician noted online registration failed to load at 8:40 a.m., and video lessons for older pupils were cancelled. At the clinic, electronic patient records were unreachable, pharmacy counter card payments failed, and staff used cash alongside paper forms for fourteen morning appointments. Ferry services experienced online booking disruptions affecting sailings, requiring staff to issue handwritten tickets at the quay, though the morning sailing still departed on time.

The incident at Harnsey Fish Works on Lantern Quay in Thornwick Sands began at about 1:50 a.m. on a Thursday in July, when a gas leak was detected in Cold Store 2. The fixed detector panel in that store registered its first high-level alarm at 1:48 a.m., and its peak reading reached 38 percent of the lower explosive limit before the readings fell below the alarm threshold at 3:05 a.m. The Shift Log records 14 workers on shift in the plant when the alarm sounded. Odile Brandt, the night shift supervisor, heard the detector horn from the packing hall and ordered the cold store staff out. She reported that nobody presented symptoms to her at the muster point beside the ice plant. The plant's suspected gas leak was logged with the Thornwick Sands Gas Board at 1:56 a.m., and a gas board engineer was assigned to the incoming propane supply line. Although the engineer reached the cold store doors before the brigade crew arrived on the quay, Tomas Verrill's crew was the first to enter the store, doing so in breathing apparatus, and the brigade later established a cordon extending about 60 meters from the doors. The packing hall extraction fans were switched off on Brandt's instruction, and the crew declared the cold store clear for re-entry after taking readings at its doorways. Frozen stock was moved from Cold Store 2 to Cold Store 1 later that morning. Two refrigerated trucks from Rennick Haulage were waiting at the loading dock when the alarm began. Both left the quay gate before 2:20 a.m. without their loads, and the loading dock remained closed for a period the records describe differently, with the Shift Log citing about two hours and the Rennick Haulage Gate Ledger citing about four hours.

The incident at Kestrel Ridge Observatory began when the grid supply to the site dropped out at 00:58 and the standby generator started automatically about twenty seconds later. The generator ran for 38 minutes before it shut down at 01:36 while the grid remained out. The controller recorded a stop event followed by a lockout state requiring a manual reset at the generator panel. Sources disagree on the cause of the shutdown. The site engineer, Talwen Pryce, attributed the stop solely to overheating protection tripping after snow blocked the cooling air intake, while night operator Imre Soller attributed it solely to low oil pressure protection tripping. The fuel tank gauge record shows 61 percent at 01:00 and 48 percent at 02:00, with no sudden drop in level between 01:00 and 02:10, which suggests fuel supply was not the cause. The dome shutter had been closed at 00:50 because of incoming snow, and the access road was closed by snow that night, which limited outside assistance. Pryce walked the 300 metres from the staff cottage through the snow in about ten minutes, reset the lockout, and restarted the unit at 02:04. Accounts also differ on the order of the power loss. Soller reported that the control room lights went out and the dome drive fell silent while the battery-backed computers stayed on. Shift handover notes state that the control room lighting went out first and the dome drive lost power only afterward, while Soller's account describes the dome drive losing power first. The uninterruptible power supply carrying the telescope control computers was rated for about 25 minutes of runtime, which is shorter than the outage duration. The handover notes also record that the generator's last routine test run was 11 days before the storm. Visiting astronomer Dr. Odalys Renk was in the visitor wing preparing data and reported that corridor lights went dark when the generator noise faded.

The Screening Line 3 hold-baggage x-ray conveyor at Tessarine Bay Airport stopped at 11:26 on a Sunday and did not return to normal throughput until mid-afternoon. The Screening Line 3 Drive Controller Event Record logged a motor overcurrent trip on the entry belt at 11:26:09, with motor current reading 31 amps at the first trip against a rated 24 amps, and two further overcurrent trips on the same belt later that morning. The Security Operations Desk Log shows a maintenance electrician was called to the screening hall at 11:34. Supervisor Odalys Merrin stated that the electrician opened the drive cabinet beside the entry belt and that the cabinet smelled warm, and she reported hearing the belt grind down and seeing about a dozen bags stacked at the x-ray tunnel mouth. The screening hall was closed to non-staff from 11:40 until the line was cleared.

Line 3 was fully out of service for about 75 minutes according to the Baggage Control Room Log, although Merrin's statement gives an estimate of about 50 minutes before bags moved through it again. The Baggage Control Room Log records that Line 3 was cleared for normal throughput at 14:40. During the stoppage, bags from check-in desks 40 to 62 were redirected to Line 2, which has lower capacity than Line 3, while Screening Lines 1 and 2 remained in service throughout. Security staff hand re-screened bags during the stoppage; the Security Operations Desk Log and Merrin's statement give different counts of 46 and 29 respectively, and the discrepancy should be reconciled. A manual re-screening procedure had also been requested for bags flagged by the x-ray software before the stop. Passengers were asked to remain near check-in until bag status was confirmed on two delayed flights.

Marlen Ground Handling's Ramp Dispatch Sheet lists four departures with baggage loading started later than planned that afternoon, and the final affected flight of the bank pushed back at 15:12. Marlen placed two extra loaders at the screened-bag chute to speed up movement once screening resumed. Operations should review the drive cabinet condition, the cause of the repeated overcurrent trips, and the reconciliation of hand re-screening counts.

Incident Report: Varnholt Swing Bridge Closing Failure, Early March

On a Tuesday in early March, the Varnholt Swing Bridge was closed to all road and foot traffic after its rotating span came to rest about 14 centimetres short of full seating on the rest piers. The span stopped at 09:52 according to the position encoder, while the Operations Log records the stop at 10:04. The encoder record shows the span rotating to 90 degrees open and later returning to within a small margin of its closed angle without reaching the final seated value. Bridge operator Imre Valtonen, on duty in the control cabin, had started the opening sequence for the sailing barge Marl Heron. The barge, 31 metres long, passed through the channel opening without contact with the fender piles. After the opening, a second closing attempt was made. The span moved less than one centimetre before the motor current limit tripped, and the encoder record confirms this movement. Valtonen reported that the closing motor ran at normal pitch but the end-of-travel light stayed unlit, and he telephoned the port engineer's on-call line after the second attempt. Both road barriers were lowered before the opening began and remained down after the failed seating. At the east barrier, seven vehicles were queued when the span came to rest, and a cyclist, Tobias Renwick, was waiting there on his bicycle. Pedestrians were allowed to walk back from the barrier along the eastern footway to the quay road. Harbourmaster Odile Brandvik ordered a vessel hold so that no further barges would be passed until the bridge was resolved, and the channel remained closed to vessels through the evening. Buses were held at the Varnholt Green stop while drivers were briefed, and the number 6 service was diverted by way of the Quillon Ring Road, adding roughly 20 minutes to the route.

On a Thursday in May, at 1:26 p.m., the freight elevator in the Finishing Building stopped between the second and third floors while travelling upward. Teodor Bram was in the car with a cart of fabric bolts. The controller recorded a safety-circuit stop command and a load of 1,140 kilograms; the unit’s rated capacity was 1,500 kilograms. Bram used the in-car call button and contacted the security desk through the intercom. The desk logged the call at 1:27 p.m.

Imogen Pask went to the third-floor landing and spoke with Bram through the closed outer doors. Dorrel Vance signed in at the gate at 1:48 p.m., went to the roof machine room, and isolated the elevator’s main power supply. He manually released the brake in short steps to lower the car to the second-floor landing. Accounts differ on the duration: Bram reported about 25 minutes, while the security desk log indicates about 40 minutes. Bram stepped out at the second floor unhurt. Pask moved the remaining fabric bolts to the third floor using the stairs and small passenger lift.

The work order identifies the elevator as a traction freight unit, notes its last scheduled inspection was in March, and records that it was tagged out of service until the following morning. The controller log shows the safety circuit reset after power was restored at 8:05 a.m. the next day. The stated causes conflict: the work order attributes the stop to the overspeed governor tripping on the upward run, while Vance attributes it to a worn third-floor door interlock contact.

The main fibre link between Skerrin Isle and the mainland failed at 11:52 p.m. on a Tuesday in late October. It normally carries 1,000 megabits per second. Monitoring recorded a total loss of optical signal in a single reading, without a gradual decline beforehand; no signal returned during the night. The 20-megabit-per-second microwave backup began carrying island traffic at 11:53 p.m. The on-duty engineer opened a priority-two incident ticket at 12:20 a.m. and activated the backup link at that time. The ticket records a repair ship requested from the mainland depot, but no confirmed arrival date.

The backup kept some services running, but its limited capacity disrupted island operations. At 7:30 a.m., the clinic administrator found electronic patient records unreachable. The clinic used paper forms for 14 morning appointments, and failed card payments meant the pharmacy counter accepted cash only until the afternoon. At 8:40 a.m., the school’s online registration system would not load, and video lessons for older pupils were cancelled because the backup could not carry them.

Ferry staff prepared handwritten ticket forms. The 9:15 a.m. sailing departed on time with paper tickets issued at the quay. Online booking was unavailable for the first four of the day’s six sailings and returned before afternoon departures. The harbour master reported calm overnight seas, winds below 10 knots, and no vessels anchored near the cable route after dark. The available facts do not establish the cause of the fibre failure.

Water from the overflowing rooftop cooling tank entered the Vessel Hythe Land Registry basement server room shortly after 01:30 on 22 October, following about six hours of heavy rain. The tank holds roughly 12,000 litres and supplies the building’s air-conditioning loop. The Basement Water Sensor Array first registered water at sensor 3 near the east wall at 01:36; by 01:41, all six floor sensors had reported water.

While making rounds on the ground floor, night security guard Ines Okafor heard water in the basement stairwell. She opened the basement door and saw about 4 centimetres of water spreading across the server room floor. The stairwell lights were working, although corridor emergency lighting had switched on. Records conflict on the first alarm time: the guard’s account gives 01:39, while the facilities report records 01:44. The facilities report also places the first sensor reading three minutes before its alarm, which does not align with the sensor array’s 01:36 reading.

Okafor called the Hythe Fire Service, giving the basement entrance on Cordwain Lane as her location, and phoned IT Systems Lead Tomas Brandl. Working remotely from home, Brandl began a controlled database-server shutdown. The sump pump started at 01:38, but its controller recorded a high-level fault at 02:05 and reduced output; it ran continuously until 05:20. Reports also conflict on peak water depth: Brandl recorded 9 centimetres, while the fire service call record states 15 centimetres. The fire crew arrived with a portable pump and left at 03:50. Only the two lowest rack-mounted storage units were touched by standing water. The 00:50 backup had completed, and no title records were lost. Public counters remained closed the following morning.

The fixed detector panel in Cold Store 2 first registered a high-level alarm at 1:48 a.m. On a Thursday in July, a gas leak was detected there at about 1:50 a.m. Odile Brandt heard the detector horn from the packing hall and ordered cold store staff out. The Shift Log records 14 workers on shift at the start of the alarm. Brandt said nobody reported symptoms to her at the muster point beside the ice plant. The detector panel’s peak reading was 38 percent of the lower explosive limit.

The plant reported a suspected leak to the gas board at 1:56 a.m., and a gas board engineer was assigned to the incoming propane supply line. Accounts differ on arrival order: Brandt said the engineer reached the cold store doors before the brigade arrived on the quay; brigade commander Tomas Verrill said his crew reached the doors before the engineer arrived on the quay. The brigade set up a cordon extending about 60 meters from the doors and entered the store wearing breathing apparatus. After taking readings at the doorways, the crew declared it clear for re-entry. Panel readings fell below the alarm threshold at 3:05 a.m.

Two Rennick Haulage refrigerated trucks were waiting at the dock when the alarm began; both left before 2:20 a.m. without their loads. The Shift Log records the dock remained closed for about two hours, while the Gate Ledger indicates about four hours. Frozen stock was moved to Cold Store 1 later that morning. The Shift Log also notes that packing hall extraction fans were switched off on Brandt’s instruction.

The basement sump pump started at 01:38, but a high-level fault at 02:05 caused it to run at reduced output until 05:20. Okafor also called the Hythe Fire Service from the Cordwain Lane entrance. The first wet reading was registered by sensor 3 near the east wall at 01:36, and by 01:41 all six floor sensors in the server room had reported water. The first flood alarm reached the guard's console at 01:39, three minutes after the first floor sensor reading. Night security guard Ines Okafor, who was on her rounds on the ground floor, heard water running in the stairwell to the basement, opened the basement door, and saw water about 4 centimetres deep spreading across the server room floor. She called the Hythe Fire Service, giving her location as the basement entrance on Cordwain Lane. Registry IT Systems Lead Tomas Brandl began a controlled shutdown of the database servers from a remote terminal after Okafor phoned him, and the title database was taken down as an emergency measure. Brandl reported that the nightly backup had finished at 00:50, so no title records were lost, and that only the two lowest rack-mounted storage units were touched by standing water. The basement sump pump started at 01:38 and ran continuously until 05:20, with a high-level fault recorded at 02:05 after which it operated at reduced output. The water on the server room floor peaked at 9 centimetres according to Brandl, and at 15 centimetres according to the Fire Service record. One engine crew attended with a portable pump and left the site at 03:50. The building's public counters remained closed for the whole of the following morning.

Varnholt Swing Bridge was closed to all road and foot traffic on a Tuesday in early March after its rotating span stopped about 14 centimetres short of full seating on the rest piers. The span came to rest short of the piers at 09:52 according to the position encoder record, and the operations log gives the time as 10:04. The encoder record measured the 14-centimetre shortfall at the span's free end. Operator Imre Valtonen was on duty in the control cabin and started the opening sequence for the sailing barge Marl Heron, a 31-metre vessel that passed through the channel opening without contact with the fender piles. Road barriers on both approaches were lowered before the opening began. When the span came to rest, four or seven vehicles were queued at the east barrier, depending on the account, and pedestrians were later allowed to walk back from the barrier along the eastern footway to the quay road. Valtonen attempted a second closing. The closing motor ran at normal pitch, but the end-of-travel light stayed unlit. During the second attempt the span moved less than one centimetre before the motor current limit tripped, and the encoder record confirms this movement. Following the second attempt, Valtonen telephoned the port engineer's on-call line. Harbourmaster Odile Brandvik ordered a vessel hold on the channel so that no further barges would pass until the bridge was resolved, and she stated that the channel remained closed to vessels through the evening so the span could be left partly closed. Barriers were left down after the failed seating. At the Varnholt Green stop, buses were held while drivers were briefed on the diversion, and the number 6 service was routed by way of the Quillon Ring Road, adding roughly 20 minutes to the route.

The fire at the Veltrane Dye Depot began in the cold-storage annex on the Orsel Canal wharf shortly after 04:00 on 22 October. The Orsel Wharf Fire Brigade log records the first alarm in the annex at 04:11 and shows that the first pumper left its station at 04:14. The annex smoke detector panel recorded an alarm on zone 2 before any other zone reported, and its backup battery took over when mains power to the annex failed at 04:17. Cameras on the north wharf lost power at 04:31, which ended coverage of the annex's canal side. Night supervisor Imre Dallow stated that the annex's refrigeration compressors had been running normally during his walk-round at 03:30.

The annex held about 40 pallets of powdered pigment and refrigerated dye concentrate, according to insurance loss adjuster Teodor Quill. Quill estimated that the annex roof collapsed entirely and that the main warehouse suffered only smoke and water damage. Firefighters drew water from the Orsel Canal using a floating suction hose. The brigade closed the wharf road to traffic until mid-morning to allow hose lines to cross it.

The timeline indicates a gap between the detector alarm and the first alarm recorded in the brigade log, and the cause of the fire is not established by the material reviewed here. The loss of camera coverage at 04:31 means canal-side observations for the early stage of the fire are unavailable from that system. Operations should reconcile the detector panel timestamps with the brigade log and the compressor status checks before drawing conclusions about the origin or spread of the fire.

The incident at Kestrel Ridge Observatory began with a grid supply outage at 00:58, after which the standby generator started automatically about 20 seconds later. The generator ran for 38 minutes before shutting down at 01:36 while the grid supply remained out. The controller recorded a stop event followed by a lockout state requiring a manual reset at the generator panel. The sources disagree on the cause of the shutdown: the site engineer attributes it solely to overheating protection tripping after snow blocked the cooling air intake, while the night operator attributes it solely to low oil pressure protection tripping. The fuel gauge record shows no sudden drop in tank level between 01:00 and 02:10, which indicates that fuel exhaustion was not the cause, though the level fell from 61 percent at 01:00 to 48 percent at 02:00. The site engineer, who lived in a staff cottage about 300 metres away, walked to the main building through the snow in roughly ten minutes, reset the lockout, and restarted the unit at 02:04. The single access road to the ridge was closed by snow that night, which limited outside assistance. The dome shutter had been closed at 00:50 because of incoming snow, before the power cut. Sources also disagree on the order of power loss: the night operator reports that the dome drive lost power first and the control room lighting went out afterward, while the handover notes report the reverse. The uninterruptible power supply carrying the telescope control computers was rated for about 25 minutes of runtime, and the handover notes list the generator's last routine test run as 11 days before the storm. The sequence and root cause should be verified against the controller data before corrective actions are set.

Screening Line 3, the hold-baggage x-ray conveyor at Tessarine Bay Airport, stopped at 11:26 on a Sunday after the Drive Controller Event Record logged a motor overcurrent trip on the entry belt at 11:26:09. According to the Baggage Control Room Log, the line was fully out of service for about 75 minutes before any bags moved through it again. The Security Operations Desk Log shows a maintenance electrician was called to the screening hall at 11:34. The same drive controller record shows two further overcurrent trips on the entry belt later that morning, indicating the fault recurred after the initial restart attempts and was not resolved by a single intervention.

While the line was down, bags flagged by the x-ray software before the stop were routed to manual re-screening, as requested in the Security Operations Desk Log. Screening Hall Supervisor Odalys Merrin reported that security staff hand re-screened 29 bags during the stoppage. Passengers were asked to remain near check-in until their bag status was confirmed on two delayed flights, according to Merrin's statement. Marlen Ground Handling placed two extra loaders at the screened-bag chute to speed movement once screening resumed, as recorded on its Ramp Dispatch Sheet. That sheet also shows the final affected flight of the bank pushed back at 15:12, which marks the practical end of the disruption to departures.

The operations review should examine the root cause of the repeated entry-belt overcurrent trips, the time taken to dispatch maintenance, and whether the manual re-screening and passenger communication steps can be carried out faster in future stoppages.

The incident was a gas leak detected in Cold Store 2 of Harnsey Fish Works on Lantern Quay in Thornwick Sands at about 1:50 a.m. on a Thursday in July, as recorded in the Harnsey Fish Works Shift Log. The fixed ammonia-propane detector panel in Cold Store 2 registered its first high-level alarm at 1:48 a.m., and its peak reading was 38 percent of the lower explosive limit. The Thornwick Sands Gas Board dispatch record shows an engineer assigned to the plant's incoming propane supply line, and according to night shift supervisor Odile Brandt, the gas board engineer reached the cold store doors before the brigade crew arrived on the quay.

The Thornwick Sands Fire Brigade set up a cordon on Lantern Quay extending about 60 meters from the cold store doors, as reported by crew commander Tomas Verrill. Crew commander Verrill also stated that the brigade took readings at the cold store doorways and then declared the cold store clear for re-entry. The Rennick Haulage Gate Ledger shows both trucks leaving the quay gate before 2:20 a.m. without their loads. Brandt reported that no one reported symptoms to her at the muster point beside the ice plant.

Following the incident, the Shift Log records that frozen stock in Cold Store 2 was moved to Cold Store 1 later that morning. The operations team should review the sequence of alarm, engineer response, cordon, clearance, and stock movement, and should confirm the timing of the brigade's re-entry declaration against the detector readings and the gas board's account of the supply line work.

The derailment of freight train 7114 occurred on the Osterby curve of the Kestrel Branch at about 05:40 on a Tuesday in early March. The train had left Kestrel Junction with two locomotives and 26 cars, and the control log records that the signal at the curve displayed a clear aspect as the train approached. A wayside detector at Milepost 41 registered the train passing at 38 miles per hour about 6 miles before the curve and recorded no overheated axle bearings on any car. Engineer Dalia Ronk applied the emergency brake after feeling a sudden lurch through the cab floor, and dispatcher Imre Voss halted all traffic on the Kestrel Branch after the emergency brake call came in. Voss's call to the maintenance office followed shortly after the alert.

Seven cars left the rails, three of them lying on their sides on the embankment. Two crew members rode in the lead locomotive and both walked away without needing transport. The ambulance crew arrived at the curve 19 minutes after the call and treated Ronk for a bruised shoulder at the scene. Fourteen of the 26 cars carried timber, and bundles from two of the overturned cars slid down the embankment toward the river's edge. Several bags of fertilizer split open on the slope, and the spilled product was shoveled into containers.

Maintenance crews used two heavy cranes to lift the overturned cars and replaced about 90 meters of track once the cars were cleared. The line reopened at 14:10 on Thursday according to the control log, while the maintenance report gives a reopening time of 21:30 on the same day, a discrepancy the operations team should reconcile. The cause of the derailment is not established by the material reviewed here.

The main fibre link between Skerrin Isle and the mainland failed at 11:52 p.m. on a Tuesday in late October, and the monitoring system recorded a total loss of optical signal in a single reading with no gradual decline beforehand. No optical signal returned on the main link at any point during the night. The backup radio link began carrying island traffic at 11:53 p.m., one minute after the failure, though its rated capacity of 20 megabits per second is far below the island's normal main-link capacity of 1,000 megabits per second. The on-duty engineer opened the incident ticket at 12:20 a.m., classed it as priority two, and the backup link was activated after the ticket was opened. The ticket lists a repair ship as requested from the mainland depot, with no arrival date confirmed. Harbour Master Tobias Reld reported that the sea was calm overnight with winds below 10 knots and that he saw no vessels anchored near the cable route after dark.

The effects were felt across the island the next morning. Nessa Okonkwo, the clinic administrator, found the clinic's electronic patient records system unreachable at 7:30 a.m., and the clinic switched to paper forms for its 14 morning appointments. Card payments at the pharmacy counter failed, so staff accepted only cash until the afternoon. At the school, IT technician Priya Venn reported that the online registration system would not load at 8:40 a.m., and video lessons for the older pupils were cancelled because the backup link could not carry them. At the ferry office, online booking was unavailable for the first four of the six sailings, returning before the afternoon departures. The 9:15 a.m. sailing departed on time with paper tickets issued at the quay, and staff had prepared handwritten ticket forms in advance.

The incident occurred at approximately 3:05 p.m. on a Friday in mid-July, when a pallet of chlorinating solution jugs fell from a forklift and split open in the loading yard of Mirelle Bay Pool Supply. According to warehouse supervisor Neve Aldersgate, warehouse staff placed sand bags around the drain before the fire service arrived, in an effort to limit the spread of the liquid. The business park air monitor first registered chlorine above its alarm threshold at 3:12 p.m. The driver, Oskar Penhallow, stated that he had remained in his cab until a worker told him to move the truck out of the yard. The fire service washed the remaining liquid with water into a temporary holding bund set across the yard, as recorded in the Tessin Fire Service incident report. The air monitor dropped below its alarm threshold at 5:05 p.m.

Supervisor Neve Aldersgate attributed the cause directly to the loading practice: the pallet fell solely because the jugs were stacked and wrapped unevenly, so the load shifted off the forks. The report identifies this as the primary factor requiring follow-up. The operations team should review stacking and wrapping standards for chlorinating solution, confirm that forklift operators are trained to inspect loads before lifting, and assess whether the yard's drainage and containment arrangements are adequate for a spill of this size. The delay between the spill and the alarm threshold being reached, as well as the driver's extended stay in the cab, should also be examined as part of the review of emergency response and personnel instructions.

The freight elevator in the Finishing Building of the Lindqvist Textile Mill stopped between the second and third floors at 1:26 p.m. on a Thursday in May. The controller log recorded a stop command from the safety circuit at that time while the car was travelling upward. The car's load cell registered 1,140 kilograms at the moment of the stop. Teodor Bram, the cart operator, was riding in the car with a cart of fabric bolts. He pressed the in-car call button and reached the security desk through the intercom, and the security desk logged that call at 1:27 p.m. Imogen Pask, the finishing floor supervisor, went to the third-floor landing and spoke to Bram through the closed outer doors. Bram stepped out at the second floor and was unhurt. Pask moved the remaining fabric bolts to the third floor by the stairs and the small passenger lift.

Dorrel Vance, the elevator technician, signed in at the gate at 1:48 p.m., arrived at the machine room on the roof, and isolated the main power supply to the elevator. He then lowered the car by manually releasing the brake in short steps until it reached the second-floor landing. Sources differ on how long the car was stalled. Bram put the time at about 25 minutes, while the security desk log records about 40 minutes. The controller log shows the safety circuit reset after power was restored at 8:05 a.m. the next day.

The work order identifies the elevator as a traction freight unit with a rated capacity of 1,500 kilograms and notes that its last scheduled inspection was in March. It also records that the elevator was tagged out of service until the following morning. The work order attributes the stop to the overspeed governor tripping on the upward run, while Vance attributes it to a worn door interlock contact on the third-floor landing door. Both are described as the sole cause, so the operations team should reconcile these findings before closing the incident.

The business park air monitor first registered chlorine above its alarm threshold at 3:12 p.m., reached its highest reading of 4.1 parts per million at 3:40 p.m., and dropped below the threshold at 5:05 p.m. A tanker from a licensed waste contractor collected the contained liquid the next morning. The driver reported staying in his cab until a worker told him to move the truck out of the yard.

The hold-baggage x-ray conveyor at Tessarine Bay Airport, Screening Line 3, stopped at 11:26 on a Sunday and did not return to normal throughput until mid-afternoon. The Screening Line 3 Drive Controller Event Record shows motor current on the entry belt reading 31 amps at the first trip against a rated 24 amps. Two further overcurrent trips on the entry belt occurred later that morning. The pattern of repeated overcurrent events points to a drive or load problem on the entry belt that was not resolved by a single reset.

Security staff hand re-screened bags during the stoppage. The figures in the available records differ: the Security Operations Desk Log records 46 bags, while the statement from Screening Hall Supervisor Odalys Merrin records 29 bags. The discrepancy should be reconciled before the figure is used in any final count.

The Marlen Ground Handling Ramp Dispatch Sheet lists four departures with baggage loading started later than planned that afternoon. The redirection to a lower-capacity line and the hand re-screening both contributed to the delay in getting bags to the ramp.

Recommended follow-up includes inspecting the entry belt drive and its motor current draw, reconciling the re-screened bag count across the two records, and reviewing the redirection procedure for check-in desks when Line 3 is down.

One engine crew attended with a portable pump and left the site at 03:50. The building's public counters remained closed for the following morning.

The Varnholt Swing Bridge was closed to all road and foot traffic on a Tuesday in early March after its rotating span stopped about 14 centimetres short of full seating on the rest piers. The position encoder recorded the stop at 09:52, while the Operations Log records it at 10:04, a discrepancy that should be reconciled during review. Bridge operator Imre Valtonen had started the opening sequence for the 31-metre sailing barge Marl Heron, which passed through the channel without contact with the fender piles. A second closing attempt followed. The span moved less than one centimetre before the motor current limit tripped, and the encoder confirms this movement. Valtonen reported that the closing motor ran at normal pitch while the end-of-travel light remained unlit, and he telephoned the port engineer's on-call line after the second attempt. Buses were held at the Varnholt Green stop during driver briefings, and the number 6 service was diverted via the Quillon Ring Road, adding roughly 20 minutes to the route.

The main fibre link between Skerrin Isle and the mainland failed at 11:52 p.m. on a Tuesday in late October. The Corran Telecom network monitoring system recorded a total loss of optical signal in a single reading, with no gradual decline beforehand, which suggests a sudden physical or equipment fault rather than progressive degradation. However, the incident ticket records that the engineer activated the backup radio link at 12:20 a.m. after the ticket was opened, which indicates manual intervention was needed to bring the link fully into service. The gap between the automatic and manual figures should be reviewed. The normal main-link capacity is 1,000 megabits per second, and the reduced capacity of the radio backup constrained services throughout the outage.

Harbour Master Tobias Reld reported calm sea conditions overnight, with winds below 10 knots, and observed no vessels anchored near the cable route after dark, so no obvious external cause in the marine environment has been identified. Online booking was unavailable for the first four of the six sailings that day and returned before the afternoon departures. The 9:15 a.m. sailing departed on time, with paper tickets issued at the quay. The clinic switched to paper forms for its 14 morning appointments, and the school's online registration system would not load at 8:40 a.m., as reported by technician Priya Venn.

**Incident Report: Gas Leak Detection, Cold Store 2, Harnsey Fish Works**

At approximately 1:48 a.m. on a Thursday in July, the fixed ammonia-propane detector panel in Cold Store 2 at Harnsey Fish Works, Lantern Quay, Thornwick Sands, registered its first high-level alarm, with a peak reading of 38 percent of the lower explosive limit. Brigade crew members entered the cold store wearing breathing apparatus, took readings at the doorways, and declared it clear for re-entry. The detector panel readings fell below the alarm threshold at 3:05 a.m. Two refrigerated trucks from Rennick Haulage, waiting at the loading dock when the alarm began, left the quay gate before 2:20 a.m. without their loads. Records differ on how long the loading dock remained closed, with the shift log citing about two hours and the gate ledger about four hours. Later that morning, frozen stock was moved from Cold Store 2 to Cold Store 1. The discrepancy in closure duration should be reconciled before the review is finalized.

At about 3:05 p.m. on a Friday in mid-July, a pallet of chlorinating solution jugs fell from a forklift and split open in the loading yard of Mirelle Bay Pool Supply. The forklift was carrying the pallet from a delivery truck to the covered dock when it tipped. The yard camera recorded the pallet leaving the forks at 3:04:50 p.m. The truck had entered the yard at 2:48 p.m., according to the gate log, and the pallet carried 48 jugs of liquid chlorinating solution, each holding 20 litres. Accounts differ on the cause of the fall. The driver, Oskar Penhallow, stated that the pallet fell solely because the forklift's front wheel dropped into a broken section of yard paving, while warehouse supervisor Neve Aldersgate stated that the pallet fell solely because the jugs were stacked and wrapped unevenly so the load shifted off the forks. Both accounts are recorded here, and the cause has not been resolved by the material reviewed. Accounts also differ on the number of jugs that burst: Aldersgate described seven, while the Tessin Fire Service Incident Report recorded eleven. Several jugs landed on the concrete and burst, and the liquid spread toward a drain at the low edge of the yard. Warehouse staff placed sand bags around the drain before the fire service arrived, and a licensed waste contractor's tanker collected the contained liquid the next morning. The camera shows two warehouse workers walking away from the spill upwind within a minute of the fall. The driver stated that he stayed in his cab until a worker told him to move the truck out of the yard. The fire service logged the call at 3:09 p.m. and the first engine reached the yard at 3:17 p.m. Firefighters in breathing apparatus righted the surviving jugs, moved them under a tarpaulin at the dock, and washed the remaining liquid with water into a temporary holding bund set across the yard. The business park air monitor first registered chlorine above its alarm threshold at 3:12 p.m., reached its highest reading of 4.1 parts per million at 3:40 p.m., and dropped below the alarm threshold at 5:05 p.m.

The first emergency call, placed by a passing canal barge pilot, was logged by dispatcher Pira Voss at 04:12, and the brigade's first pumper left its station at 04:14. Voss's record notes that the caller reported flames visible through the annex's upper vents. Security camera footage time-stamped 04:09 shows the annex roller door glowing orange along its lower edge. Cameras on the north wharf lost power at 04:31, so coverage of the annex's canal side ends at that point. The annex detector panel moved to backup battery when mains power to the annex failed at 04:17.

Night supervisor Imre Dallow was the only supervisor on site. He reported that the annex refrigeration compressors were running normally during his 03:30 walk-round. He led six warehouse staff out through the loading door, and his headcount in the yard confirmed that all shift personnel were accounted for within minutes of evacuation.

Five appliances were on site at the peak of the response according to Voss's record, while the brigade log records four. Firefighters drew water from the Orsel Canal using a floating suction hose. One firefighter was treated for a minor wrist burn and returned to duty. The brigade closed the wharf road to traffic until mid-morning to allow hose lines to cross it. Insurance loss adjuster Teodor Quill estimated that the annex roof collapsed entirely and that the main warehouse sustained only smoke and water damage. The annex held approximately 40 pallets of powdered pigment and refrigerated dye concentrate.

The grid supply to Kestrel Ridge Observatory dropped out at 00:58, and the standby generator started automatically about twenty seconds later. The generator ran for 38 minutes before shutting down at 01:36 while the grid remained out. The generator controller recorded a stop event followed by a lockout state requiring a manual reset at the generator panel. Accounts differ on the cause of the shutdown. The site engineer, Talwen Pryce, reports that the generator stopped solely because its overheating protection tripped after snow blocked the cooling air intake. The night operator, Imre Soller, reports that it stopped solely because its low oil pressure protection tripped. The fuel gauge record shows the tank at 61 percent at 01:00 and 48 percent at 02:00 with no sudden drop, so fuel exhaustion does not appear to be a factor.

Accounts also differ on the sequence of power loss within the building. Imre Soller reports that the dome drive lost power first and the control room lighting went out afterward, while the shift handover notes state the reverse. Visiting astronomer Dr. Odalys Renk reports that the visitor wing corridor lights went dark as the generator noise faded. The dome shutter had been closed at 00:50 because of incoming snow, before the power cut. The single access road was closed by snow that night, and the last routine generator test run was 11 days before the storm. Talwen Pryce walked from the staff cottage to the main building in about ten minutes, reset the lockout, and restarted the generator at 02:04. The telescope control computers were carried by an uninterruptible power supply rated for about 25 minutes of runtime, which is a relevant margin to note in reviewing the event.

The detector panel’s readings fell below its alarm threshold at 3:05 a.m. After taking readings at the doorways, the brigade crew declared the cold store clear for re-entry. The loading dock remained closed for about four hours after the alarm began.

Freight train 7114 derailed on the Osterby curve of the Kestrel Branch at about 05:40 on a Tuesday in early March. The train had 26 cars, including 11 carrying timber.

About six miles before the curve, the train passed the wayside detector at Milepost 41 at 38 miles per hour. The detector recorded no overheated axle bearings on any car.

Engineer Dalia Ronk reported feeling a sudden lurch through the cab floor and then applied the emergency brake. Two crew members were riding in the lead locomotive. Both walked away from the wreck without requiring transport. Ambulance crew treated Ronk at the scene for a bruised shoulder.

The available facts establish the event timing and location, the train’s recorded speed at the detector, and the crew’s response and immediate condition. They do not identify the cause of the lurch or derailment. The detector’s bearing readings provide no indication of overheated axle bearings when the train passed Milepost 41; they do not establish conditions at the curve.

On a Friday in mid-July, a delivery truck entered the Mirelle Bay Pool Supply yard at 2:48 p.m. carrying 48 jugs of liquid chlorinating solution, each holding 20 litres. The supervisor reported seven burst jugs; the fire service incident report recorded eleven.

Several jugs landed on the concrete and burst, sending liquid toward a drain at the yard’s low edge. Within a minute, the camera showed two workers walking away from the spill upwind. The driver said he remained in his cab until a worker told him to move the truck. Warehouse staff placed sand bags around the drain before firefighters arrived. The fire service logged the call at 3:09 p.m.; its first engine reached the yard at 3:17 p.m.

The air monitor first exceeded its alarm threshold at 3:12 p.m., peaked at 4.1 parts per million at 3:40 p.m., and fell below the threshold at 5:05 p.m. Firefighters wearing breathing apparatus righted surviving jugs, moved them under a tarpaulin, and washed remaining liquid into a temporary holding bund. A licensed waste contractor collected the contained liquid the next morning.

The service effects documented in the supplied records include unavailable online ferry booking and failed card payments at the clinic pharmacy. At the pharmacy counter, staff accepted cash only until the afternoon.

The ferry office record indicates that the sailing proceeded despite the booking outage. Harbour Master Tobias Reld reported calm seas overnight and winds below 10 knots; these conditions are noted but do not establish a cause for the link failure.

The incident ticket lists a repair ship as requested from the mainland depot, but no arrival date is confirmed. The supplied information does not state when the fibre link will be repaired or whether the backup link’s capacity was sufficient for island traffic during the outage. Operations should track the repair ship’s status and confirm service restoration and any remaining constraints.

Water on the server room floor reached a peak depth of 15 centimetres, and the title database was shut down as an emergency measure.

The timing of the initial detection is inconsistent across the records. The facilities incident report places the first floor sensor reading before the first alarm reached the guard’s console at 01:44. The discrepancy should be reconciled against the original alarm and sensor logs to establish the response timeline.

The Sump Pump Controller Log records the basement sump pump starting at 01:38 and running continuously until 05:20. Okafor called the Hythe Fire Service; the call record gives her location as the basement entrance on Cordwain Lane. The available information does not establish when the overflow began, when the water was fully cleared, or when the title database was restored.

On a Thursday in May at 1:26 p.m., the Finishing Building freight elevator stopped between the second and third floors while travelling upward. Teodor Bram was in the car with a cart of fabric bolts. Dorrel Vance signed in at the gate at 1:48 p.m., went to the roof machine room, and isolated the elevator’s main power supply. He lowered the car by manually releasing the brake in short steps until it reached the second-floor landing. Bram stepped out there unhurt. The accounts differ on how long the car was stuck: Bram estimated about 25 minutes, while the security desk log records about 40 minutes.

The stated cause is also disputed. The work order attributes the stop solely to the overspeed governor tripping during the upward run; Vance attributes it solely to a worn third-floor landing-door interlock contact. The elevator was tagged out of service until the following morning. The controller log shows the safety circuit reset after power was restored at 8:05 a.m. the next day. Pask moved the remaining fabric bolts to the third floor using the stairs and small passenger lift.

Operator Imre Valtonen reported that the closing motor sounded normal, but the end-of-travel light remained unlit. Records disagree on when the first alarm was raised: the brigade log gives 04:11, while the annex detector panel records 04:06, with zone 2 activating first. Security footage shows an orange glow at the roller door’s lower edge at 04:09. The first emergency call was logged at 04:12 from a passing canal barge pilot, who reported flames visible through the upper vents. The first pumper left its station at 04:14.

The detector panel indicates that mains power failed at 04:17 and its backup battery took over. North wharf camera coverage of the annex’s canal side ended at 04:31 when the cameras lost power. The fire response used a floating suction hose to draw water from the canal. Records differ on peak attendance: the brigade log reports four appliances, while the dispatcher’s call record reports five.

Imre Dallow was the only supervisor on site. He led six warehouse staff through the loading door, and his headcount accounted for everyone on shift in the yard within minutes. Dallow reported that the refrigeration compressors had been running normally during his 03:30 walk-round. The annex contained about 40 pallets of powdered pigment and refrigerated dye concentrate. The loss adjuster estimated that the annex roof collapsed entirely; the main warehouse sustained smoke and water damage. One firefighter received treatment at the scene for a minor wrist burn and returned to duty. The wharf road remained closed until mid-morning to allow hose lines to cross it.

At about 01:30 on 22 October, water from an overflowing rooftop cooling tank entered the basement server room at the Vessel Hythe Land Registry. The tank holds roughly 12,000 litres and supplies the air-conditioning loop. Heavy rain had fallen for about six hours beforehand.

The first wet reading was recorded by east-wall sensor 3 at 01:36. The guard’s account places the first alarm at 01:39, three minutes later; the facilities incident report records it at 01:44, several minutes after the first sensor reading. By 01:41, all six server-room floor sensors had detected water. The sump pump started at 01:38 and ran continuously until 05:20, but its controller recorded a high-level fault at 02:05, after which it operated at reduced output.

During rounds on the ground floor, night guard Ines Okafor heard water running in the basement stairwell. She reported that the stairwell lights were working, while emergency lighting had switched on in the corridor. On opening the basement door, she saw approximately 4 centimetres of water across the server-room floor. The recorded peak depth is inconsistent: the IT systems lead reported 9 centimetres, while the fire service call record states 15 centimetres.

Okafor called the Hythe Fire Service and gave her location as the basement entrance on Cordwain Lane. One engine crew attended with a portable pump and left at 03:50. After Okafor called him, IT systems lead Tomas Brandl initiated a controlled remote shutdown. The two lowest rack-mounted storage units were the only equipment touched by standing water. The 00:50 nightly backup had completed, and no title records were lost. Public counters remained closed the following morning.

At about 3:05 p.m. on a Friday in mid-July, a pallet of chlorinating solution fell from a forklift in the loading yard of Mirelle Bay Pool Supply. The truck had entered the yard at 2:48 p.m. The forklift was moving the pallet from the truck to the covered dock when it tipped. The load contained 48 jugs, each holding 20 litres. The camera recorded the pallet leaving the forks at 3:04:50 p.m.

Accounts conflict on the cause and extent of the spill. The driver attributed the fall solely to a forklift wheel dropping into broken paving; the warehouse supervisor attributed it solely to unevenly stacked and wrapped jugs shifting off the forks. The supervisor reported seven burst jugs, while the fire service recorded eleven. Several jugs struck the concrete, and liquid spread toward a drain. Within a minute, two workers were seen walking away from the spill upwind. The driver said he remained in his cab until a worker told him to move the truck.

The air monitor first exceeded its alarm threshold at 3:12 p.m., peaked at 4.1 parts per million at 3:40 p.m., and fell below threshold at 5:05 p.m. The fire service logged the call at 3:09 p.m. and arrived at 3:17 p.m. Firefighters in breathing apparatus righted surviving jugs and sheltered them under a tarpaulin. They washed remaining liquid into a temporary holding bund. Before the fire service arrived, warehouse staff had placed sandbags around the drain. A licensed waste contractor collected the contained liquid the next morning.

The site lost grid supply at 00:58, and the standby generator started automatically about 20 seconds later. It stopped at 01:36, after running for 38 minutes, while the grid remained out. The dome shutter had been closed at 00:50 because of the incoming snow. The observatory sits on a ridge served by a single access road, which was closed by snow that night.

The cause of shutdown is disputed. Site engineer Talwen Pryce attributed it solely to the overheating protection tripping after snow blocked the cooling air intake; night operator Imre Soller attributed it solely to the low oil pressure protection tripping. The controller log records a stop event followed by a lockout requiring manual reset, but does not resolve these conflicting accounts. The fuel gauge fell from 61 percent at 01:00 to 48 percent at 02:00, with no sudden drop recorded between 01:00 and 02:10.

Accounts also conflict on the order of the power effects: Soller said the dome drive lost power before the control room lights went out, while the shift handover notes state the reverse. Soller was the only operator on duty and reported that battery-backed computers stayed on. In the visitor wing, Dr. Odalys Renk reported corridor lights going dark as the generator noise faded.

Pryce walked from the staff cottage, about 300 metres away, through the snow in roughly ten minutes, reset the lockout at the generator panel, and restarted the unit at 02:04. The UPS supporting telescope control computers was rated for about 25 minutes. The last routine generator test was 11 days before the storm.

Screening Line 3, the hold-baggage x-ray conveyor, stopped at 11:26 on Sunday after its entry-belt drive controller recorded an overcurrent trip. The first trip registered 31 amps against a rated 24 amps; two further overcurrent trips were recorded later that morning. Supervisor Odalys Merrin reported hearing the belt grind down and seeing about a dozen bags stacked at the x-ray tunnel mouth. She also said an electrician opened the drive cabinet beside the entry belt, which smelled warm.

A maintenance electrician was called at 11:34. The screening hall was closed to non-staff from 11:40 until Line 3 was cleared. Bags from check-in desks 40 to 62 were redirected to Line 2, which had lower capacity; Lines 1 and 2 remained in service. The logs differ on how long Line 3 was out before bags moved through it again: the Baggage Control Room Log records about 75 minutes, while Merrin’s statement gives about 50 minutes. The Baggage Control Room Log records clearance for normal throughput at 14:40.

Security requested manual re-screening of bags flagged by x-ray software before the stoppage. The reported hand re-screening totals also differ: 46 bags in the Security Operations Desk Log and 29 in Merrin’s statement. Marlen Ground Handling added two loaders at the screened-bag chute. Its dispatch sheet lists four departures with baggage loading later than planned; the final affected flight pushed back at 15:12. Merrin said passengers on two delayed flights were asked to stay near check-in until their bag status was confirmed.

Freight train 7114 derailed on the Osterby curve of the Kestrel Branch at about 05:40 on a Tuesday in early March. It had left Kestrel Junction with two locomotives and 26 cars. The signal at the curve displayed a clear aspect. About six miles before the curve, the train passed the Milepost 41 detector at 38 miles per hour; the detector registered no overheated axle bearings.

Engineer Dalia Ronk felt a sudden lurch through the cab floor and applied the emergency brake. Shortly after the emergency brake alert, dispatcher Imre Voss received the call and halted all traffic on the branch. Seven cars left the rails, three overturning on the embankment. Bundles of timber from two overturned cars slid toward the river’s edge, and fertilizer bags split open on the slope.

Two crew members rode in the lead locomotive; both walked away without needing transport. The ambulance crew arrived 19 minutes after the call and treated Ronk at the scene for a bruised shoulder.

Recovery required two heavy cranes to lift the overturned cars. Crews replaced about 90 meters of track after clearing the cars. Spilled fertilizer was shoveled into containers. The line reopened at 14:10 on Thursday, though another report states it reopened at 21:30 that day; the discrepancy requires reconciliation.

The Varnholt Swing Bridge was closed to road and foot traffic on a Tuesday in early March after its rotating span failed to seat on the rest piers. The Operations Log records the span at rest at 10:04, while the encoder record gives 09:52; the discrepancy remains unresolved. The encoder shows the span rotated to 90 degrees open before returning to within a small margin of its closed angle, stopping 14 centimetres short of the seated value at the free end.

Operator Imre Valtonen initiated the opening sequence for the sailing barge Marl Heron. He reported that the closing motor ran at normal pitch, but the end-of-travel light did not illuminate. A second closing attempt moved the span less than one centimetre before the motor current limit tripped. Valtonen then called the port engineer’s on-call line. Road barriers on both approaches had been lowered before the opening and remained down after the failed seating.

The 31-metre Marl Heron passed without contacting the fender piles. Harbourmaster Odile Brandvik ordered a vessel hold, and the channel remained closed through the evening with the span partly closed. Reports differ on the east-barrier vehicle queue: cyclist Tobias Renwick counted four vehicles, while Valtonen reported seven. Renwick said pedestrians could walk back along the eastern footway to the quay road. Buses were held at Varnholt Green while drivers were briefed on the diversion. Number 6 service was rerouted via Quillon Ring Road, adding roughly 20 minutes.

Two refrigerated trucks at the loading dock left before 2:20 a.m. without their loads. Records differ on the closure period: the Shift Log states about two hours, while the Rennick Haulage Gate Ledger records about four. Later that morning, frozen stock was moved to Cold Store 1. The Shift Log also records that Brandt instructed staff to switch off the packing hall extraction fans.

The main fibre link between Skerrin Isle and the mainland failed at 11:52 p.m. on a Tuesday in late October. Corran Telecom’s monitoring system recorded an immediate total loss of optical signal, with no preceding decline. The signal did not return overnight. The link normally provides 1,000 Mbps. Monitoring records show that the 20 Mbps backup radio link began carrying island traffic at 11:53 p.m.; however, the incident ticket says the on-duty engineer opened a priority-two ticket and activated the backup at 12:20 a.m. This discrepancy should be reviewed.

The outage affected essential services the following morning. At 7:30 a.m., clinic administrator Nessa Okonkwo found electronic patient records unavailable. Staff used paper forms for 14 morning appointments, and the pharmacy counter accepted cash only until the afternoon after card payments failed. At 8:40 a.m., the school’s online registration system would not load. Video lessons for older pupils were cancelled because the backup link lacked sufficient capacity.

Ferry operations continued with contingency paperwork. The 9:15 a.m. sailing departed on time using paper tickets issued at the quay. Online booking was unavailable for the first four of six sailings and returned before afternoon departures. The incident ticket records a request for a repair ship from the mainland depot but gives no confirmed arrival date. Harbour Master Tobias Reld reported calm seas, winds below 10 knots, and no vessels anchored near the cable route after dark.

At 1:26 p.m. on a Thursday in May, the Finishing Building freight elevator stopped between the second and third floors while travelling upward. Teodor Bram was inside with a cart of fabric bolts. The controller log recorded a safety-circuit stop command and a load of 1,140 kilograms. The maintenance work order lists a rated capacity of 1,500 kilograms and a scheduled inspection in March.

Bram pressed the in-car call button and contacted the security desk by intercom. The desk logged the call at 1:27 p.m. Imogen Pask went to the third-floor landing and spoke with him through the closed outer doors. Vance signed in at the gate at 1:48 p.m., isolated the main power supply in the roof machine room, and manually released the brake in short steps to lower the car to the second-floor landing. The duration is disputed: Bram estimated about 25 minutes, while the security desk log records about 40 minutes.

Bram exited unhurt. Pask moved the remaining fabric bolts to the third floor using the stairs and small passenger lift. The work order records that the freight elevator was tagged out of service until the following morning. The controller log shows the safety circuit reset after power was restored at 8:05 a.m. the next day.

The recorded cause remains unresolved. The work order attributes the stop to an overspeed governor trip during the upward run; Vance attributes it to a worn third-floor landing-door interlock contact.
